explain.say: Forging shapes metal by hammering or pressing it, usually while it glows hot. Steel is forged at around 1,100 to 1,250 degrees Celsius, where it is soft like stiff clay but still solid.

faq.q: How hot is metal for forging?
faq.a: Steel is usually hot forged at about 1,100 to 1,250 degrees Celsius, glowing yellow-orange. Some small parts are cold forged at room temperature, which needs much bigger forces.
asks: Do blacksmiths have to heat metal?

faq.q: What does hammering do to the metal inside?
faq.a: Hammering breaks coarse grains into finer ones, closes up tiny voids, and pushes the metal's structure to follow the shape. Finer grains make metal both stronger and tougher.

Grain flow is the direction the metal's grains are stretched during forging. When grains follow the outline of a part, cracks find it hard to cut across them, just as wood is hard to split across its grain.
asks: Why does the grain direction matter?

faq.q: What is the difference between forging and casting?
faq.a: Casting pours liquid metal into a mould; it can make complicated shapes but may trap bubbles and has random grains. Forging squeezes solid metal into shape, giving denser metal with grains that follow the part.
asks: Forged or cast, which is better?

faq.a: Crankshafts and connecting rods in engines, spanners and hammers, aircraft landing gear, railway wheels and many bolts are forged because they must take heavy, repeated loads.

facts: Smiths forged iron by hand for thousands of years before steam hammers arrived in the 1840s.
Modern hydraulic forging presses can push with forces of tens of thousands of tonnes.
